sentences: Write the country code at your first stop after the border, at the nearest possible stopping place.
If you cross by ferry or train, write it at the port or station of arrival.
On the disc, the guidance note sets this order:
1. Under the inner time dial, just under the time at which you stopped (or arrived at the port or station).
If a reference line marks where you opened the tachograph, put the code under that line.
You don't need to write the date, because the sheet already has a place for it.
2. If there isn't enough room there, write it between the inner and outer time dials, to the left of the reference line (or where one would be), without damaging existing or future recordings.
3. Only as a last resort, write it on the back of the disc, adding the crossing time in 24-hour format (for example "20:30").
You only need to make this entry when you enter a Member State.
Use the official nation codes, for example "B" for Belgium and "D" for Germany.

sentences: A 'break' is any period in which you may not drive or do any other work, and which you use only to recover.
After 4.5 hours of driving you must take an uninterrupted break of at least 45 minutes, unless you take a rest period.
You can split it into at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30 minutes.
On occasional passenger services, it can instead be two breaks of at least 15 minutes each.
In multi-manning, you may take the 45-minute break in the moving vehicle as long as you are not helping the driver.

Time spent travelling to or from a vehicle that is not at your home or your employer's base does not count as a break, unless you are on a ferry or train with access to a sleeper cabin, bunk or couchette.

sentences: Yes, but only in limited cases.
You may go over the driving and rest limits (Articles 6 to 9) only as far as you need to reach a suitable stopping place.
This is allowed only if road safety is not put at risk and the extra driving is needed for the safety of people, the vehicle or its load.
You must write the reason by hand on the record sheet, on a tachograph printout or in the duty roster.
Do this at the latest when you arrive at the stopping place.
Any extra time must be made up with an equal period of rest, taken in one block together with a rest period, by the end of the third week after the week in question.
Commission guidance note 1 (December 2007, older than the current Regulation) says you cannot use this for reasons known before the trip started.
It must be an unexpected situation outside your control, such as a major accident, extreme weather, a road diversion or a full parking area.
Enforcers check that it is not a regular habit.
The note also says the extra driving must not shorten your breaks or your daily and weekly rest.
Separately, in exceptional circumstances you may drive up to 1 extra hour to reach your employer's operational centre or your home for a weekly rest.
You may drive up to 2 extra hours if you took an uninterrupted 30-minute break just before, and only to start a regular weekly rest there.

sentences: Not automatically.

Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 (consolidated 31.12.2024) allows a short departure from the driving and rest rules only if road safety is not jeopardised, only to the extent needed to ensure safety of persons, the vehicle or its load, and to reach a suitable stopping place.
You must record the reason manually on the tachograph record sheet, printout or duty roster at the latest on arrival at that stopping place.
The Commission guidance note 1 (December 2007) is older than the current act, so follow the act where they differ.
It says the derogation is for unexpected, unavoidable situations, not regular ones, and that you must not gain time by exceeding driving limits while looking for parking.
The passages do not say whether a traffic jam by itself qualifies, and the note says carriers should plan for regular traffic jams, so any stop-over on that ground is judged on the facts.

sentences: The AETR replaces Regulation 561/2006 for international road transport operations that are carried out partly outside the areas covered by the Regulation.
It then applies as follows:
- If the vehicle is registered in the EU (Community) or in a country that is a contracting party to the AETR, the AETR applies for the whole journey.
- If the vehicle is registered in a third country that is not an AETR contracting party, the AETR applies only to the part of the journey made on EU territory or in AETR contracting countries.
The AETR rules are meant to be aligned with the Regulation, so that its main provisions still apply, through the AETR, to the part of the journey made inside the EU.

sentences: A daily rest taken on a ferry or train may be interrupted no more than twice, and the interruptions may total no more than one hour.

Under the Commission guidance note, when the daily rest is split into two parts (at least 3 hours and at least 9 hours), the two-interruption limit applies to the whole daily rest period, not to each part separately.

The guidance note is older (January 2017, before the 2020 Mobility Package), so the current Regulation 561/2006 Article 9(1) governs, and the twice-and-one-hour limit in that Article matches the note.
The note's two-part point is not restated in the current Article text.
The driver must also have access to a sleeper cabin, bunk or couchette during the rest.

sentences: Your daily rest can be interrupted no more than twice in total.
The limit covers the whole daily rest, not each part, so you do not get two interruptions in the 3-hour part and two more in the 9-hour part.
The interruptions are for other activities such as embarking or disembarking.
Together they must not exceed 1 hour, and they must not reduce your daily rest.
During the rest you must have access to a sleeper cabin, bunk or couchette.
The point about split rest comes from a Commission guidance note from 2017, which is older than the 2020 rule changes.
The current Regulation still allows at most two interruptions totalling one hour, so the two do not conflict on this.

Under Regulation 561/2006, a transport undertaking is liable for infringements committed by its drivers, even when the infringement was committed in another Member State or a third country.
So a Swedish company can be held responsible for a rest-period infringement its driver committed in Germany.

sentences: Generally yes.
Driving a vehicle on public roads, laden or empty, to a garage, a car wash or a fuel station counts as carriage by road under Regulation 561/2006.
This applies whether you are a temporary or a permanent driver.
There is one exception.
The rules cover drivers engaged in carrying goods or passengers by road.
If your job, by its nature, does not include transporting goods or passengers, you may fall outside the Regulation's scope.
Even then, your Member State may still apply the same rules to you under national law.
This explanation comes from a Commission note from 2012, which is older than the 2020 Mobility Package changes.
However, the current Article 1 still limits the rules to drivers engaged in carrying goods and passengers.

Under Regulation (EC) No 561/2006, Article 13(1), each Member State may grant exceptions from Articles 5 to 9 for listed categories of vehicles, and point (r) lists vehicles used for the delivery of ready-mixed concrete.

The exception may apply on the Member State's own territory or, with the agreement of the States concerned, on another Member State's territory, subject to individual conditions and provided the objectives in Article 1 are not prejudiced.
Member States must inform the Commission of exceptions granted under Article 13(1), and the Commission informs the other Member States.
